grants.title: Countywide Resilience Planning Program
grants.summary: Supports counties in developing plans to address climate change vulnerabilities and implement sustainable projects.
grants.description: The Countywide Resilience Planning Program provides support to counties in New York State to develop comprehensive plans that address vulnerabilities to climate change, including coastal flooding and other environmental risks. The program emphasizes sustainable project implementation and the use of natural infrastructure to reduce risks. Counties are encouraged to engage in inclusive planning processes that involve community stakeholders. The program aims to enhance the resilience of social, economic, and ecological systems. Interested counties can learn more and apply through the Department of State's website.
grants.eligibility_notes: Eligible applicants are counties within New York State.
key_requirements: Applicants must be counties within New York State.
Proposals must address climate change vulnerabilities.
Plans should include sustainable project implementation.

Resilience Planning
Improving resilience to climate change impacts on the natural and built environment as well as social and economic systems.
NEW! Environmental Bond Act at DOS
Overview
The Office of Planning, Development and Community Infrastructure works with communities to increase their resilience to climate change impacts, particularly coastal flooding. The Office employs key
resilience principles
that help communities understand their vulnerabilities, advance resilience measures that reduce risk, including through the use of natural infrastructure and natural processes, and avoid investments that are not highly adapted to a changing climate. The Office provides this assistance in ways that also acknowledge the added stress on communities from development pressures and broader socioeconomic forces.
Climate Adaptation
Assess
Sea level rise, changes in water levels, and more frequent intense storms associated with climate change increase the vulnerability of communities already at risk from flooding and storm surge. Understanding physical risk and identifying the assets at risk and which have high community value helps a community manage future risks and avoid consequential (or unacceptable) impacts.
Learn more
Decide
Proactive planning can help avoid and reduce the negative impacts of climate change, accounting for a range of future climate scenarios and community choices while also identifying and taking advantage of the potential benefits.  The Office advocates for an inclusive process that is accessible to all members of the community and leads to decisions that are widely-supported and achievable.
decision process
Implement
Risk reduction measures encompass a variety of non-structural, soft-structural, and structural techniques, including avoidance of current and projected hazards through improved land use. An adaptive implementation process incorporates flexibility into long-term risk management by allowing for changes in community priorities, available information, and the nature of the risk.
implementation process
Resilience
Programs
Resilience is the capacity for a community and its ecosystem to withstand extreme events and other forces or risks; quickly recover the interconnected social, economic and ecological systems’ structure and function in the aftermath of a disaster; and develop ongoing adaptability to rapidly changing environmental conditions and forces.

grants.title: Local Waterfront Revitalization Program (LWRP)
grants.summary: This grant funds the development and implementation of Local Waterfront Revitalization Programs to address waterway issues, improve water quality, and promote public waterfront access in New York State.
grants.description: The Local Waterfront Revitalization Program (LWRP) is New York State's primary program for partnering with waterfront communities to address local and regional waterway issues. It aims to improve water quality, guide development to areas with adequate infrastructure, promote public waterfront access, and redevelop underutilized waterfronts. Municipalities can apply for funding to develop and implement long-term plans for their waterfront areas. The program involves a three-tier approval process: local adoption, state approval, and federal concurrence. Once approved, municipalities are eligible for implementation funds to execute prioritized projects.
grants.eligibility_notes: Eligible applicants are municipalities in New York State with waterfront areas.
key_requirements: Applicants must be municipalities in New York State.
Projects must address local or regional waterway issues.
Plans must include long-term land and water use strategies.
Approval requires local, state, and federal concurrence.

Local Waterfront Revitalization
The LWRP is the State’s primary program for working in partnership with waterfront communities across New York State.
Overview
The Local Waterfront Revitalization Program (LWRP) serves as the Office of Planning and Development’s primary program for working in partnership with waterfront communities across the State to address local and regional (coastal or inland) waterway issues, improve water quality and natural areas, guide development to areas with adequate infrastructure and services away from sensitive resources, promote public waterfront access, and provide for redevelopment of underutilized waterfronts.
How it Works
Plan
LWRPs begins with a planning process that centers on developing a vision for the future of the waterfront.
Execute
LWRPs are approved on three levels of government through local adoption; Secretary of State approval; and federal concurrence from NOAA’s Office of Coastal Management for coastal LWRPs.
Implement
Once an LWRP is approved and in place, municipalities are eligible for implementation funds through the Local Waterfront Revitalization Program to begin to implement identified and prioritized projects.

grants.title: Brownfield Opportunity Area (BOA) Program
grants.summary: This grant funds community-based plans to redevelop brownfields and other vacant or abandoned sites, transforming them into properties that facilitate community investment and improvement.
grants.description: The Brownfield Opportunity Area (BOA) Program provides grant funding and technical assistance to communities for developing area-wide, community-based plans to redevelop brownfields and other vacant or abandoned sites. The program supports planning, state designation, and implementation phases, enabling municipalities and private sector partners to realize redevelopment goals. Designated BOA communities are eligible for additional state funding and assistance to jumpstart redevelopment. The program aims to empower communities to revitalize neighborhoods affected by brownfields. Interested applicants can learn more through the Department of State's website and resources.
grants.eligibility_notes: Eligible applicants include municipalities and community organizations seeking to redevelop brownfields and other vacant or abandoned sites.
key_requirements: Applicants must be located in New York State.
Projects must focus on brownfield redevelopment or revitalization of vacant/abandoned sites.
Applicants must demonstrate community support for the proposed plan.

Brownfield Redevelopment
Empowering communities to revitalize neighborhoods affected by brownfields.
Overview
The Brownfield Opportunity Area (BOA) Program provides communities grant funding and technical assistance to develop area-wide, community-based plans to effectively redevelop brownfields and other vacant and abandoned sites, transforming them into catalytic properties that facilitate community investment and improvement.
How It Works
Planning
Brownfield redevelopment begins with a planning process that enables communities to articulate a clear vision, goals, and strategies for redevelopment of brownfield sites and broader community revitalization.
Designation
State Designation of a Brownfield Opportunity Area affirms the commitment of communities and New York State to realize the vision and goals established during the planning process.
Implementation
With a community-supported plan in place, municipalities and private sector partners can begin to realize the vision and goals of the BOA plan. Designated BOA communities are eligible to access additional State funding and assistance to jumpstart the redevelopment process.

grants.title: Local Government Training Program
grants.summary: This program provides training in land use planning, regulation, and local governance for local officials in New York State.
grants.description: The New York Department of State’s Local Government Training (LGt) program offers workshops and online courses to teach land use planning, regulation, and local governance to local elected and appointed officials. The program benefits members of planning boards, zoning boards of appeals, elected officials, enforcement officials, and other municipal employees. Training is available both on-site and online, with interactive courses and recorded webinars. Members of planning boards and zoning boards of appeals are required by state statute to complete four hours of training annually. To schedule a workshop or obtain assistance, contact the program at 518-473-3355.

Overview
The New York Department of State’s Local Government Training (LGt) staff teaches land use planning and regulation and local governance and procedure to local elected and appointed officials annually at regional and county workshops across the state.
The staff is also available to assist members of planning boards, zoning boards of appeals, local governing boards, and municipal staff with technical information, explanations, tips, and examples of successful approaches to land use and other local regulation. Members of planning boards and zoning boards of appeals are required by state statute to obtain four hours of training a year.
All on-site and online interactive training courses offered by local government training staff count toward this requirement.
To discuss scheduling a training workshop or obtain other assistance, call the Local Government Training program at 518-473-3355.

▪New York State is transitioning grants management activities from the Grants Gateway to the 
Statewide Financial System (SFS) on January 16, 2024 . 
•SFS is New York State (NYS) government’s accounting and financial management system used to manage 
contracts andpayments.
▪State Agencies who are using the Grants Gateway today will transition to using SFS for those business 
processes they are currently performing in the Grants Gateway.​
▪Grantees will transition to using SFS to create and submit prequalification applications and may also use 
SFS to support other aspects of the grants management business process (e.g., searching for bid 
opportunities, responding to bids, approving grant contracts, submitting claims), depending on the work they 
are doing with agencies.​
▪Following the transition, the Grants Gateway will be retired.​
▪Key components of the grants management business process remain the same , with the 
understanding that there will be some differences in the way SFS supports the business process, given it is a 
different system.Grants Management in SFS Transition

Grants Gateway Data Conversion
▪Many Gateway transactions will be converted to the new system. The following slides describe the type 
of transactions and components that will be converted. It is important to note that relatively large 
amounts of data will remain accessible only via the Gateway. Examples are included in upcoming slides.
▪Grantees will have approximately 6 months following go -live to download and store any historical 
information not converted to SFS. Thereafter, access will be further restricted. Additional details will be 
shared as they become available.

9 Contents subject to change. ||
Conversion: Prequalification
▪If a Grantees Grants Gateway Document Vault is in a “Prequalified” status at go -live, the following 
components of their MOST RECENT APPROVED prequalification application will be converted:
•Prequalification Status
•Prequalification Expiration Date
•Responses to Organization Capacity, Compliance, and Integrity Questions
•Required Documents
▪Supporting materials such as Status Change history and previous prequalification applications will not 
be converted.
▪Grantees that are NOT prequalified at go -live must complete this requirement in SFS.  Regardless of 
prior Prequalification history, no materials will be converted.

10 Contents subject to change. ||
Conversion: Grant Opportunities / Applications
▪A limited number of State agency grant opportunities may be active or available for online application in 
the Grants Gateway at go -live.  Such opportunities will not be converted to SFS; but rather allowed to run 
their course.  Note, any resulting contracts will be processed in SFS.
▪Only successful grant applications that resulted in a contract developed and executed in the Gateway will 
be converted.  In such cases, only the Gateway’s Application PDF will be converted.  Examples of 
applications and materials that will not be converted include:
•Applications started but not submitted
•Applications submitted but not funded
•Applications funded by any mechanism other than a Grants Gateway contract
•Status Change and Workflow histories
•Any materials captured during the application process including comments and uploads not included 
in the Application PDF

11 Contents subject to change. ||
Conversion: Progress Reports and Payments
▪Progress Reports:
•Progress reports initiated, submitted and/or approved in the Grants Gateway will not be converted.
▪Payments:
•Grantees that participated in online claiming in the Gateway can expect:
•Only approved Grants Gateway payments will be converted.
•Payments not approved at go -live will need to be reentered in SFS.
•Period -specific budget category balances will be derived from converted claims.
•The Grants Gateway Payment PDF will be available for review in SFS.
•Additional Information such as Status History, comments, and any uploads not included in the 
Payment PDF will not be carried forward to SFS.

12 Contents subject to change. ||
Conversion: Contracts and Amendments
▪In Process Contracts, e.g., Contracts that have not been fully executed:
•Grantees that are actively negotiating and signing contract(s) in the Gateway prior to go live can expect to 
resume work in SFS post cutover.  The following points are noteworthy:
•Contracts will retain their Grants Gateway contract number.
•Contracts will inherit the newly updated NYS Grant Contract Template.
•Signatures accumulated in the Grants Gateway will be erased.
•Contract properties including budget and workplan data will be carried forward to avoid reentry.
•Additional information such as Status Change History, Comments, and Document Uploads will not be 
available and may need to be manually reentered or uploaded and reattached in SFS.
▪Approved Contracts:
•All contracts approved in the Grants Gateway will be converted. Note:
•Contracts will retain their Grants Gateway contract number.
•The fully executed Contract Document (PDF) will be converted.
•Contract properties including budget and workplan data will be carried forward to avoid reentry in the 
event the contract is amended.
•Additional information such as Status Change History, Comments, and Document Uploads will not be 
available and/or need to be manually reentered or uploaded and reattached in SFS.

 I. INTRODUCTION  
 
The New York State Department of State’s Office for New Americans (DOS/ONA) was created in 2012 
to welcome immigrants and to help them in achieving their American dream. Through its statewide 
network of community-based providers, ONA assists all new Americans in accessing and navigating a 
variety of free services and supports their inclusion as an integral part of New York State’s diverse cultural 
fabric.  
 
Since 2014, ONA has offered mobile English programming to new Americans across the State. Through 
this Request for Applications (“RFA”) ONA is seeking to build on this work by establishing an expanded 
mobile English program to meet the needs of diverse new Americans across the state, particularly assisting 
new Americans who have limited English proficiency, representing over 13% of all New Yorkers. 
 
This RFA seeks a qualified provider to develop and maintain a mobile English platform that allows 
students to access ESOL lessons through mobile devices. The grantee will also provide on demand 
coaching and support for navigating lessons offered in the platform and promote the program through 
development of outreach materials and training of staff at ONA and ONA partner organizations. 
 
 
II. APPLICANT ELIGIBILITY 
 
Minimum Requirements 
 
1. Applicants may be a for-profit or not-for-profit organization with the ability to do business in New 
York State. Not-for-profit organizations shall mean any not-for-profit corporation exempt from 
taxation under Section 501(c)(3) of the internal revenue code.   
2. Not-for-profit applicants must be pre-qualified through the Statewide Financial System 
(https://grantsmanagement.ny.gov/register-your-organization-sfs ) as of the application due date listed on the cover of this RFA.  
 
 
III. FUNDING AND PROJECT PERIOD  
 
The initial contract period under all parts of this RFA is anticipated to be one year with the option of two 
additional one-year renewals. Funding in the subsequent years is contingent upon funds being 
appropriated in the State budget, performance, and the organization’s ability to meet the program 
requirements as stipulated in this RFA.  
 
 
IV. GENERAL PROGRAM SERVICES 
 
The purpose of this RFA is to identify an organization which will provide English lessons and courses 
available through mobile devices to new Americans in New York State.   
 

   
2 
 The target population for these funds are immigrants, regardless of status, residing or working in New 
York and in need of mobile English language classes. The contractor must verify that users reside or 
work in New York State before any services are delivered under this grant.  The contractor will also 
provide support to ONA partner organizations assisting immigrants who fall within the criteria listed 
above. 
 
All services provided under this grant must be offered at no charge to clients and ONA partner 
organizations. 
 
V. REQUIRED ACTIVITIES  
 
This section discusses required activities and contractual documentation requirements for the mobile 
English contractor funded under this RFA.  
 
Services must adhere to NY Information Technology Services (ITS) Security Policies and Standards , 
including accessibility of information communication technology for individuals with disabilities.1 
The Contractor must ensure that all State Data related to this Contract is stored within the Continental 
United States (CONUS), in a controlled access environment to ensure data security and integrity. State 
Data refers to all client/user information collected or generated by technology or staff working on this 
grant, lessons and training modules. All access to State Data, physical or virtual, must be conducted within 
CONUS and have adequate security systems in place to protect against the unauthorized access to the 
facilities and data stored therein. The Contractor shall not send or permit to be sent to any location outside 
of the CONUS, any State Data related to this Contract. Contractor will provide the State a list of the 
physical locations where the Data is stored at any given time and will update that list if the physical 
location changes. Access into and within the facilities must be restricted through an access control system 
that requires positive identification as well as maintains a log of all accesses (e.g., date and time of the 
event, type of event, user identity, component of the information system, outcome of the event). The 
Contractor shall have a formal procedure in place for granting computer system access to the data and to 
track access. Access for projects outside of those approved by the State is prohibited. 
 
Development of a Mobile English platform must comply with:  
a. ISO 9001 – Quality Management Systems is a globally recognized standard for quality 
management. It helps organizations of all sizes and sectors to improve their performance, meet 
customer expectations and demonstrate their commitment to quality. Its requirements define how 
to establish, implement, maintain, and continually improve a quality management system (QMS). 
 
b. ISO/IEC 27001 – Information Security, Cybersecurity, and Privacy Protection is the world's best-
known standard for information security management systems (ISMS). It defines requirements an 
ISMS must meet. The ISO/IEC 27001 standard provides companies of any size and from all sectors 
of activity with guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving 
an information security management system. It promotes a holistic approach to information 
security: vetting people, policies and technology. An information security management system 
 1 https://its.ny.gov/policies . 

   
3 
 implemented according to this standard is a tool for risk management, cyber-resilience, and 
operational excellence. 
 
c. ISO/IEC 20000-1 – Information Technology – Service Management. specifies requirements for 
an organization to establish, implement, maintain and continually improve a service management 
system (SMS). The requirements specified in this document include the planning, design, 
transition, delivery and improvement of services to meet the service requirements and deliver 
value. 
 
d. NIST SP 800-163 Revision 1 – Vetting Security of Mobile Applications.  Revision 1 expands on 
the original document by exploring resources that can be used to inform an organization’s 
requirements for mobile app security.  These include overviews of relevant documentation from 
the National Information Assurance Partnership (NIAP), the Open Web Application Security 
Project (OWASP), The MITRE Corporation, and NIST. 
 
e. NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5 – Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and 
Organizations. Offers a proactive and systematic approach to cybersecurity measures for all types 
of computing platforms, including general-purpose computing, cyber-physical, cloud-based, 
weapons, space, communications, environmental control, and industrial control systems as well as 
mobile and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. 
 
If at any time, DOS becomes aware that the contractor is not compliant with current ITS policies, a notice 
of deficiency will be issued allowing a period of time to become compliant. If the contractor does not 
rectify the issue, the contract may be terminated. 
 
In addition, the contractor will ensure that clients with disabilities served under this grant have equal 
access to the Mobile English RFA program in compliance with Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act,2 as 
amended, and Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).3  The ONA Ramirez June Initiative 
will work with the contractor should they need any technical assistance related to accessibility. 
 
If awarded a contract, the Contractor will ensure that licenses will be offered no later than one (1) month 
after the start of the contract and coaching will be offered by the end of the first quarter of the contract.   
 
If a contractor is unable to meet these requirements within the specified timeframe, the State reserves the 
right to rescind the award and make a new award to the next highest scoring applicant. 
 
1. On-Going Maintenance of a Mobile English Platform 
 
Platform Overview 
 
The Contractor will be expected to develop and maintain a mobile English platform. The mobile English 
platform will allow users to learn and practice English vocabulary, grammar, spelling, writing, listening, 
and pronunciation through a series of lessons on a variety of topics.

4 
 At a minimum, the platform must be: 
a. Accessible via any type of cellular device. As not all individuals have smartphones, courses and 
coaching offered under this ONA mobile English platform must be accessible by a non-smart 
mobile phone. This platform will not need to be accessible by landline phones. 
b. Available to access lessons 24 hours a day. 
c. Easy to navigate by individuals of all digital literacy levels. 
d. Easy to navigate by all English language proficiency levels, including support for pre-literate 
individuals.  
e. Accessible for individuals including, but not limited to, deaf or hard-of-hearing clients who need 
sign language interpretation or who are using their own third-party relay interpretation services 
including video remote interpretation or Telecommunications devices for the Deaf (TDD) 
including Text Telephones (TTY). 
f. Accessible for individuals who are blind or low vision, including the use of Alt Text descriptions 
for any images on the platform, and ensuring the platform is compatible with screen reader devices.  
g. Accessible for individuals who are color blind.  
 
User Language Accessibility 
 
The interface of the platform should have a feature to translate icons, directions and instructions into 16 
ONA specified languages: 
1. Arabic 
2. Bangla 
3. Burmese 
4. Dari 
5. French 
6. Haitian Creole 
7. Korean 
8. Pashto 
9. Polish 
10. Portuguese 
11. Russian 
12. Simplified Chinese 
13. Spanish 
14. Thai 
15. Urdu 
16. Wolof 
 
Users should be allowed to indicate on the platform their preferred language choosing from any of the 
16 ONA Specified Languages listed above.  They should then be directed to the platform that is 
translated into that language. This includes instructions on how to access the platform including, but not 
limited to, registration and on-boarding information, course description, and selections.  
 
A user manual should be made available for users in any of the 16 ONA Specified Languages.  
The user manual will be required to include instructions on how to navigate and access content within the 
platform and should be accessible to individuals with all ranges of technology literacy and skill.

 Privacy 
 
The Contractor is required to have strict written and comprehensive privacy measures in place to protect 
the identity of users. All sub-contractors with access to users’ data must receive a copy of and comply 
with the Contractor’s privacy policies. 
 
2. Course Catalogue 
 
The mobile English platform should offer a wide variety of classes for users at all levels, which are 
responsive to the needs of the new Americans across New York State.  
 
The contractor should make available: 
a. courses for preliterate, beginning, intermediate, and advanced users,  
b. at least ten sector-specific English courses, and  
c. at least ten life skills courses.  
 
Additional courses may be offered as well. All courses should include a learning objective which focuses 
on the development of certain skills.  Courses should include multiple lessons that are able to be completed 
on average in 3 minutes or less, with lessons building on previous lessons in the course.  
 
Courses should positively impact community health and wellness, such as promoting age friendly job 
creation and economic stability, transportation mobility and the ability to leverage investments that can 
have complimentary benefits in more than one area. 
 
Sector specific  courses should focus on the development of English tailored for certain industries 
(including but not limited to healthcare, hospitality, banking, IT).  
 
Life skills  courses should allow users to develop English language skills to adapt to daily life in New York 
State. Life skills courses may include, but are not limited to: 
a. civics 
b. digital literacy  
c. health and well-being  
d. financial literacy  
e. parenting  
f. school 
 
Certificate 
At the end of each course, students should receive a certificate that they have successfully completed the 
course. 
 
  

   
6 
 3. Licenses 
 
Based on past usage by participants in the ONA mobile English learning program in New York State, 
5,000 total licenses are anticipated annually. If, during a given contract year, it appears that more than 
5,000 licenses are needed, prior approval must be received from DOS and the Office of the State 
Comptroller (OSC) to amend the contract to pay for the additional licenses. 
 
It is expected that the Contractor will maintain the capacity to provide 5,000 licenses at any given time. 
Priority should be given to clients utilizing services and programs within the ONA network. ONA will 
provide the Contractor with a list of affiliated providers, and it would be the Contractor’s responsibility to 
verify if a new user is working with any of those providers. The contractor must utilize a tracking system 
that sends prompts to users who have not logged into the ONA mobile English learning program for over 
a month and then suspends their license if they do not log into the ONA mobile English learning program 
within a week, thereby freeing up the license for another user.  
 
4. Coaching  
 
One or more live coaches should be available to students who need additional assistance with navigating 
or accessing the platform or completing lessons on the platform. Coaching may include support with on-
boarding, lessons, or technical support. The Contractor must have the capacity to provide coaching 
through direct contact with users in the language of the user’s choice either using staff fluent in the 
language or through use of an interpreter.  
 
The platform should have the ability to notify users that coaching is available in any language. 
 
The coach should be able to communicate with deaf and hard-of-hearing clients through third party relay 
interpreters. 
 
Coaching should be easily accessed by users. At a minimum, coaches should be available from 8 am - 
10 pm Eastern Time in order to ensure availability during peak usage hours. 
 
5. Training  
 
The contractor will offer training to users and ONA partner organizations working with the immigrant 
community on the platform. Training must include instruction on all the functions and offerings of the 
platform and how to navigate it, including how to access the reporting functions. Trainings should be 
offered at least monthly to either individual providers or a group of providers.  Trainings may be held 
virtually or in person.  
 
6. Promotional Materials 
 
At the beginning of the grant, the contractor must develop promotional materials such as a PowerPoint 
presentation, flyers, training videos, demo videos and testimonials of success (collectively “promotional 
materials”) on the mobile English program and how to access it, which can then be used by ONA staff 
and partners to share about the program. These materials must be updated quarterly or after any changes 
are made to the platform or courses. 

   
7 
  
The contractor grants ONA and ONA partner organizations a non-exclusive, perpetual, irrevocable, 
royalty free license to copy and distribute promotional materials. At a minimum, materials must be 
translated into the 16 ONA Specified Languages. The contractor shall provide draft promotional materials 
to ONA for final approval prior to distribution.    
 
7. Data and Reporting 
 
The Contractor must develop and maintain a system to generate on-demand user reports. These reports 
should contain historical data on individual learner usage including, but not limited to: 
a. affiliation with ONA partner organizations 
b. time spent accessing the platform,  
c. time spent on courses, 
d. courses completed 
e. courses engaged with  
f. last log-in.  
 
These data reports should be made available to interested ONA partner organizations to track the progress 
of their users. Data reports may only be shared with the organization with whom the user has indicated an 
affiliation.  
 
The Contractor must also be able to produce quarterly reports for ONA. The report will include: 
a. the number of licenses being used 
b. the number of active users (active users are unique users who have engaged with the platform for 
at least 30 minutes in the quarter being reported)  
c. the number of courses offered on the platform and data on course engagement and usage 
d. number of coaching hours provided 
e. interpretation services provided through coaching 
 
8.  Subcontracting 
 
For applicants engaging subcontractors to work under this grant, the lead applicant must provide the 
majority of direct programming, or more than 50 percent.   
  
As part of the application, the applicant is required to submit a signed letter of support from each of the 
proposed subcontractors, the submission or lack of submission, will be scored as part of the program 
evaluation. If awarded, any grantee intending to subcontract work under this grant is required to complete 
a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with each subcontractor that specifies all services each partner 
agrees to provide and includes the Employer Identification Number (EIN) of the subcontractor.  MOUs 
are required to be submitted to ONA prior to the start of services.

partners, consultants, or other organizations engaged and must coordinate how each subcontractor plans

Funding Strategy  
To effectively target resources and obtain the most cost-effective result, ONA has determined that the 
provision of at least 5,000 licenses (including cost of maintaining the platform and coaching hours), 
training hours, and promotional materials are the primary outcomes for which ONA will provide 
reimbursement under the contract. ONA is seeking prospective applicants who can demonstrate that they 
can provide and maintain a mobile English program to achieve these outcomes in a well-defined and cost-

offered by the platform. 
c. How the platform will be available for users to access lessons 24 hours a day.  
d. How the platform can be navigated by individuals of all digital literacy levels.  
e. How the platform can be navigated by all English language proficiency levels, including 
pre-literate individuals.   
f. How the platform is accessible for individuals including, but not limited to, deaf or hard-
of-hearing clients who need sign language interpretation or who are using their own third-
party relay interpretation services including video remote interpretation or 
Telecommunications devices for the Deaf (TDD) including Text Telephones (TTY). 
g. How the platform is accessible for clients who are blind or low vision, including the use of 
Alt Text descriptions for any images on the platform, and ensuring the platform is 
compatible with screen reader devices.   
h. How the platform is accessible for individuals who are color blind. 
 
 User Language Accessibility   
 
1. Describe how the platform provides translation or interpretation for limited English proficient 
users.   
 
2. Describe how users will be able to indicate on the platform their preferred language choosing from 
any of the 16 ONA Specified Languages listed in the Required Activities section of the RFA.  
  
3. Describe how the platform will direct the user to instructions on how to access the platform, 
including, but not limited to registration information, course description and selections in the 
language identified.  
  
4. Demonstrate that a user manual will be made available for all users in the language of their choice 
from any of the 16 ONA Specified Languages.  
 
5. Demonstrate that all lessons will be translated into all the 16 ONA specified languages listed above 
so students can connect English phrases with the meaning in one of those languages.  
 
 
 
 

   
12 
  
Privacy   
 
1. Demonstrate that written and comprehensive privacy measures are in place to protect the identity 
of users.  
 
2. Describe the process in which all sub-contractors with access to users’ data will receive a copy of 
and comply with the Contractor’s privacy policies. 
 
Course Catalogue   
 
1. Describe how the platform will offer the following courses:  
a. courses for pre-literate, beginning, intermediate and advanced English language learners 
and 
b. at least ten sector-specific courses and at least ten skills courses that respond to the needs 
of new Americans in New York State. Describe the sector-specific workforce courses and 
life skills courses.   
 
2. Describe how the courses offered will include a learning objective which focuses on the 
development of certain skills. Within that description, demonstrate that courses will include 
multiple lessons that are to be able to be completed on average in 3 minutes or less, with lessons 
building on previous lessons in the course.   
 
3. Describe how courses will positively impact community health and wellness, such as promoting 
age friendly job creation and economic stability, transportation mobility and the ability to leverage 
investments that can have complimentary benefits in more than one area. 
 
 
Certificate   
 
1. Describe how at the end of each course, the applicant will provide users with certificates 
demonstrating that they have successfully completed the course.  
  
 
Licenses & User Verification   
 
1. Describe the organization’s capacity to provide and host at least 5,000 total licenses annually.  
 
2. Describe the organization’s process for confirming users are individuals who reside or work in 
New York State.  
 
3. Describe organization’s proposed tracking system that sends prompts to users who have not 
logged into the ONA mobile English learning program for over a month and the process for 
suspending their license if they do not log into the ONA mobile English learning program within 

   
13 
 a week.  
 
 
 
Coaching   
 
1. Describe how one or more live coaches will be available to students who need additional 
assistance with the platform and the courses.  
 
2. Demonstrate that the applicant has the capacity to provide coaching through direct contact with 
users in the language of the user’s choice either using staff fluent in the language or through use 
of an interpreter.  
 
3. Describe how the coach will be able to communicate with deaf and hard-of-hearing clients 
through third party relay interpreters. 
 
4. Describe how the platform will notify users that coaching is available in all languages.  
 
5. Demonstrate that coaching will be easily accessed by users. 
 
6. Demonstrate coaches will be available from 8 am - 10 pm, Eastern Time, in order to ensure 
availability during peak usage hours.  
 
  
Trainings and Outreach   
 
1. Describe the type of training that will be offered to users and ONA partner organizations 
working with the new American community.  
 
2. Describe how training will include information on the platform, all its functions and offerings, 
and how to navigate it, including how to access the reporting functions. 
 
3. Describe how trainings will be offered at least monthly to either individual providers or a group 
of providers.   
 
4. Demonstrate ability to produce multilingual training materials in the 16 ONA Specified 
Languages which can be used by ONA and other ONA partner organizations.  
 
 
Data and Reporting

reports. 
 
2. Demonstrate that these reports will contain historical data on individual learner usage including:

f. last log-in

4. Describe how the applicant will develop quarterly reports for ONA that will include: 
a. the number of licenses being used, 
b. the number of active users (active users are unique users who have engaged with the platform 
for at least 30 minutes in the quarter being reported), 
c. the number of courses offered on the platform and data on course engagement and usage 
d. number of coaching hours provided 
e. interpretation services provided through coaching 
 
 
Promotional Materials

2. Describe the process for updating these materials quarterly or after any changes are made to the

Subcontracting

Overview
The New York State Office of Faith and Nonprofit Development Services stands as a beacon of support and resource for faith-based and nonprofit organizations across the state. With a mission deeply rooted in Governor Kathy Hochul’s commitment to support and expand these communities, the Office is dedicated to fostering growth, equity, and connectivity.
At its core, the Office aims to empower Faith and Nonprofit organizations. By providing essential information, facilitating access to state grants, and enhancing organizational capacities, it seeks to create a more inclusive and supportive environment for all New Yorkers.
Key initiatives include:
Coalition Building: Through one-on-one engagements, regional stakeholder meetings, and faith-based gatherings, the Office promotes collaboration and unity among diverse groups.
Capacity Building: Spearheaded by influential leaders like Reverend Dr. AR Bernard, this initiative focuses on interfaith dialogue and interagency collaboration to offer comprehensive support services, including mental health directories and more.
Grants and Funding: With a strategic allocation of funds, including the Governor Hochul’s Community Resource Room Grant, the Office ensures equitable distribution of resources across various community groups to support their missions and projects.
Housing Initiative: This effort seeks to leverage faith-based properties to increase housing opportunities, reflecting Governor Hochul’s commitment to growth and sustainability, while addressing New York’s housing crisis.
Community Outreach and Guide Development: Aiming for local, regional, and statewide impact, the Office develops guides on mental health, grant application processes, housing initiatives, and creating sensory-friendly spaces, tailored specifically for the faith community.
The Office of Faith and Nonprofit Development Services is more than just a resource – it is a partner in progress, dedicated to building stronger communities through faith, collaboration, and innovation.

Doreen M. Harris was appointed President and CEO of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA)
on April 7, 2021, after serving as Acting President and CEO since June 2020.
President Harris is leading NYSERDA’s role to advance the policy frameworks, clean energy technologies, and solutions to help further New York’s clean energy transition while creating hundreds of thousands of good-paying clean-energy jobs and building an equitable economy.
Under President Harris’s direction, NYSERDA is supporting New York’s clean energy initiatives through advancing infrastructure and innovation, large-scale and distributed renewables, building decarbonization, advanced nuclear, energy storage, transportation electrification, clean fuels, transmission and resiliency. Additionally, as Chair of the State Energy Planning Board, NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen M. Harris was instrumental in leading the development and finalization of a State Energy Plan in 2025 that ensures New York State has an actionable and objective framework to guide progress toward an affordable, abundant, reliable, clean energy system for all New Yorkers.
President Harris joined NYSERDA in 2010 and served as Vice President of Large-Scale Renewables, where she spearheaded the strategic development of New York’s land based renewable and offshore wind resource, including the execution of the State’s offshore wind master plan. Prior to her career in public service, President Harris spent more than a decade in the private sector, serving in management and engineering roles.
President Harris serves as chair of the State Energy Planning Board, and on the boards of the Advanced Energy Research and Technology Center (AERTC), Alliance to Save Energy, National Offshore Wind Research and Development Consortium, NY BEST and Veloz’s Public Policy Board; and is a member of the Sustainable Development Solutions Network Leadership Council and an ambassador for the Clean Energy Education and Empowerment (C3E) Initiative.
President Harris holds a Bachelor of Science in Chemical Engineering from the University of Rochester and a Master of Business Administration from the University at Albany, State University of New York.
Anzala B. Alozie is the Director of Energy & Climate with the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA)
and leads targeted efforts to ensure New York’s clean energy transition delivers equitable, economic, health and environmental benefits to historically underserved and disadvantaged communities.
In her role, Anzala’s work drives NYSERDA’s Climate Equity Strategy to achieve an inclusive clean energy economy by reducing burden and increasing benefits to historically marginalized and disadvantaged communities. Anzala directs the foci NYSERDA’s Energy and Climate Equity team which includes a suite of programs and initiatives designed for equitable and meaningful stakeholder engagement & collaboration and advancing community-driven solutions, while ensuring NYS residents have access to clean energy programs, incentives and opportunities.
